Name: Elena Gold
Question: What do you think will happen to Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich who was arrested for alleged spying in Russia?
Answer: On July 19, 2024, the Regional Court in Yekaterinburg, Russia, sentenced American journalist Evan Gershkovich to 16 years in a maximum security colony. Russian human rights activist Vladimir Osechkin says that possibly he was baited by the FSB, to facilitate his arrest. 32-year-old journalist of WSJ was found guilty of espionage for collecting information about ‘Uralvagonzavod’, which is a factory that makes tanks for the Russian army. The prosecutor asked for an 18-year sentence. Gershkovich pleaded “not guilty” and insisted that he was acting as a journalist, not a spy. The court hearings were held behind closed doors, as the prosecution alleged the information that Gershkovich was getting was a “state secret”. Only the judge, the prosecutor, the defendant and his lawyers were present. Journalists were allowed into the meeting room for a few minutes before the hearing commenced to take photos and videos. Gershkovich, with a shaved head, greeted his colleagues with a smile, but did not answer any questions. Journalists were also allowed into the courtroom for the announcement of the harsh verdict: 16 years in a maximum security prison. Evan Gershkovich was detained on March 29, 2023 in Yekaterinburg, where he arrived for the second time in a month, to continue his investigation for the next story. At the WSJ Gershkovich worked since January 2022 — he joined the respected media just a month before Russia invaded Ukraine. Since then, he authored several key news stories related to Russia and Ukraine. In early March 2023, weeks before his arrest in Russia, he and his colleagues released a story about the growing tensions between the founder of “Wagner” Yevgeny Prigozhin and the Kremlin elites. In particular, the material stated, Kremlin officials turned to Russian President Vladimir Putin with a request to “rein in” Prigozhin, who criticized the Russian Ministry of Defense. Gershkovich was also one of the authors of a high-profile WSJ article about how Putin’s entourage may be hiding truthful information from him about the war in Ukraine. Putin receives a written report from the front every morning, however, the reports emphasize Russia army’s successes, and failures are tuned down. The reports are also delayed for several days, because they have to pass filters of the FSB and the Security Council, as well as get a personal stamp of approval from Nikolai Patrushev (then the secretary of Russia’s Security Council), the article claimed. Gershkovich's materials before his arrest in March 2023 were devoted to the worsening prospects for the Russian economy, the situation around Bakhmut, the visit to Moscow of China’s leader Xi Jinping and protests over the bill on "foreign agents" in Georgia. According to the photographer who worked with Gershkovich, he was collecting material for an article about how people in Russian regions perceive the war, for which he visited Yekaterinburg and Nizhny Tagil, and planned to go to other cities. The media wrote that Gershkovich was also interested in activities of the “Wagner”, including recruitment and cemeteries of the deceased fighters. At his court process, Gershkovich did not admit guilt and insisted that his research was purely journalistic. Evan Gershkovich became the first American journalist in modern Russian history to be accused of espionage. The last time an American journalist had been detained in Russia on espionage charges was in 1986, when a “News & World Report” employee Nicholas Daniloff was arrested. Daniloff was exchanged 3 weeks later. Before his arrest, Gershkovich worked in Russia for about 6 years, since 2017. At the time of his detainment, he had been living in London but regularly traveled on business trips to Russia, where he worked as part of the WSJ's Moscow bureau. His parents Mikhail Gershkovich and Emma Milman were emigrants from the USSR, but Evan himself lived his entire life in America. Several journalists who were friends with Gershkovich said that they warned him that reporting in Russia on the topics he was picking was dangerous and he could be arrested. But obviously, he didn’t think so. Gershkovich’s name has been frequently mentioned as someone who could be exchanged to Russian spies and assassins, arrested in Europe and the USA. He is probably the highest profile American hostage held by Putin. Putin discussed exchanging Gershkovich in his interview to Tucker Carlson in February 2024. Putin wanted to get in exchange the FSB assassin Vadim Krasikov, who is imprisoned in Germany. In 2021, Vadim Krasikov was sentenced to life in prison for the murder of Chechen field commander Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin in 2019. Carlson said at the time that Putin needed to talk to Germans about it. Peculiarly, Gershkovich’s process wasn’t held in Moscow but 2 thousand kilometers away, in Yekaterinburg, where he was arrested — away from Russia’s capital, where most of the foreign correspondents reside. This obviously prevented many western ambassadors and embassy officials from attending the process, which they would likely do as a show of solidarity, if the court hearing was in Moscow. The only hope for Gershkovich to get out of the Russian prison is an agreement for an exchange, which Putin would probably only approve if his assassin Krasikov is released, and Germany doesn’t seem keen on that. Otherwise, Gershkovich may only hope to get out if Vladimir Putin, on whose order he was arrested (no doubt, such high profile arrest and prosecution would require the highest nod), is no longer the ruler of Russia. So, Gershkovich is likely to remain behind bars in Russia, as the locals call it, “for as long as Putin is alive.”

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How can I join Russian Army as a foreigner? I know I need to know Russian. Do I need to be a resident or not? Tell me all requirements for it.
Answer: “They went on the assault, and the commanders shouted to them, “Quickly! Fast! Forward!” And everyone died…” Jaroslav Halajczyk is a citizen of Slovakia. Living in the European Union, in a NATO country, he was fascinated by the distant Russia and “mysterious Russian soul.” He thought that moving to a hut somewhere in the forests of Siberia, away from civilization, would be an awesome idea. Oddly, he decided to realize his dream by participating in the war against Ukraine — a decision that he got to regret very soon. 35-year-old Yaroslav went through all the “perks” of the Russian Army: deception, lack of training, threats of being sent to a punishment pit and “nullified” (killed), as well as the slaughter of a standard Russian “meat attack”. At the military enlistment office in Moscow he was promised that he would be serving as a builder in the rear — digging, working. But in Luhansk region, their documents were taken away and all 70 of them were transferred to the assault troops. He found himself in the East Ukraine near the town of Liman, as part of many Russian infantry groups. His most shocking realization after witnessing the tactic of “meat assaults” by small groups — after which only a few of stormtroopers returned alive, was that Russians “do not value their people.” By a strike of luck, he survived a deadly attack in which most of his group were killed — and managed to surrender to the Ukrainian troops. Before signing up for the Russian army, he believed that there were Nazis in Ukraine and “Nazis are bad”. Only when he surrendered, he realized that the Russian propaganda lied — Ukrainians were normal and friendly people. He didn’t see any “Nazis”. Citizens of third countries who are thinking about signing a contract with the Russian Ministry of Defense should understand that for the Russians any “non-Russian” is cannon fodder. They are happy to take anyone — you don’t need to speak Russian, don’t need to be a resident, don’t need to even be healthy or strong — but they are only using such volunteers in “meat attacks”, throwing one human wave after another on Ukrainian positions, waiting for Ukrainians to run out of ammunition. And the Russian commanders don’t want you to survive, go home and tell the tale. They don’t need alive witnesses of their crimes. Yaroslav’s romantic ideas about Russia nearly got him killed, but he was lucky. There are many such ”romantics” in Ukrainian captivity, but even more of them are buried in the fertile Ukrainian soil.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What's wrong with most Russian people?
Answer: An old man in Bashkortostan is being sent to war, from which he is unlikely to return. Well-groomed, well-dressed officials are standing there and sending an elderly man, who clearly was forced to sign a contract because the family needs the money, to a nearly certain death. His family and friends — 2 women to the left and 2 men to the right — are also there to say ‘Good bye.” And no one is ashamed to look the poor guy in the eye. The head of the administration of the Kiginsky district posted the photo that shows the whole essence of the recruitment of volunteers. ”Thank you for your courage! Wishing you strength, luck and health, to return home safe and sound!” wrote Ruslan Vakhitov. If Vakhitov doesn’t send the allocated number of “volunteers”, he’d be in a big trouble with his superiors — delivering enough “cannon fodder” is #1 responsibility of every head of administration in 2024 Russia. Bashkiria pays 1 million rub. (USD 11,000) on sign up of an army contract — in Moscow, volunteers are paid twice as much. (Original screenshot in the comments below.) That’s how much the life of a Russian citizen is worth – $10,000–24,000, depending on the place of residence. The government pays more for the life of a Muscovite than for a resident of small Siberian towns. Young Russian men who emigrated with their wives to avoid mobilization say their mothers wanted them to go to war — even tried to report them to the military enlistment office, to stop them from leaving Russia. The oppositional Russian media outlet ‘Meduza’ tells stories of 2 men whose mothers wanted them to go to war: they wanted their sons to be “heroes” — even if the sons would be killed. The guys say the biggest motivation of their mothers wasn’t even the money — it was their own social status. Mothers were more concerned what others would think than the well-being of their sons. Sergey’s story When Russia began its mobilization campaign in the fall of 2022, Sergey protested by putting up anti-war posters. He was arrested, and after his release, he decided to emigrate with his wife and 1-year-old son. He didn’t tell his parents about it: they were avid supporters of Putin. Sergey purchased tickets and exchanged funds from rubles to dollars. It was the currency exchange receipt that his mother accidentally found — and began asking questions. Sergey told his mother they planned to leave in 2 months (they were leaving sooner, but he was hesitant to reveal the exact date, fearing that his mother might try to physically stop them). The mother was furious: ‘Why don’t you want to go defend your country? You owe it!’” Sergey was evasive, and his mother was getting more and more agitated. “It’s your duty! You’re a man! Come on — you don’t even have a good job right now! You’ll make some money, you’ll be a hero, and your son will be proud of you!” When Sergey asked whether she realized that he could be killed, she responded that “at least you’d die like a man.” “Everyone will be proud of you. Your son will see you as a hero, and your wife will be the widow of a hero.” This was so weird that Sergey didn’t even take his mother’s words seriously. But she was dead serious. She even summoned his younger brother to inform the military enlistment office about Sergey’s plans to skip the draft. “Go to the conscription office and turn him in, so that he doesn’t escape,” she instructed the younger brother. Sergey couldn’t believe it — his brother had to send him the screenshots of correspondence with the mother. Grigory’s story Grigory is also a young father. His daughter was born shortly before February 2022. When Russia began mobilization in September 2022, he decided to leave the country. When he told his mother on the phone that he was planning to leave with the wife and their child, she demanded that he’d go and fight in Ukraine. “Grigory, why would you leave? That’s a felony! Why don’t you just go, try it out?” demanded his mother. “Who knows — maybe you’ll even come back,” she added chillingly. These last words shocked the young father. “I couldn’t believe it at first,” Grigory says. “I said we had a bad connection and asked her to repeat what she’d said. Then I gave the phone to my wife, and my mother said the same thing to her.” His wife’s parents had the same opinion: they wanted their son-in-law to go to war. His mother-in-law insisted that Grigory should “go and defend his homeland”. When he asked his mother what if he were killed, she just wouldn’t respond. “What could she say? That she wouldn’t be sorry to see her own son be killed for no reason?” Grigory commented bitterly. His wife also asked his mother if she weren’t worried to lose her son, and the mother responded that “everyone is going” — and that his wife should let him go, too, because he “might return.” “The only thing she was thinking about was the social status it would supposedly bring. Based on her personality, I think she was just afraid of what people would say,” Grigory concludes. The present Both Sergey and Grigory left Russia. They now live abroad. They didn’t completely cut off communication with their parents, but the relationship is extremely strained. Basically, they only call to allow the kids chat to their grandparents. Grigory says he feels better now about the whole thing, although at first it did affect him. Sergey still talks to his father, who supports the war but didn’t try to stop him from leaving. “But not my mom: she’s blacklisted forever,” he says. “It was painful to learn that my mother wishes me dead… It was pretty hard to come to terms with the fact that the person who carried me inside her, who washed my butt when I was little, can just say: go die. But what am I losing by not seeing my mother? She didn’t have any kind of special motherly love for me. All I’m losing is the physical presence of a person who only yells at me, curses at me, and is always upset about something. And who spouted crazy fascist nonsense every day,” Sergey concludes.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What types of strategies do you suggest to optimize your Quora usage and increase views?
Answer: Good content + consistency = Quora success. “Content is king” has been the motto of internet copywriting since the World Wide Web became a thing. I’ve been writing for the Internet since 1999 — and good content has always been the key. That’s what I found out in my 6+ years of writing for Quora (and wish I knew when I just started): Quora is a great community of thinkers, with over 400 million unique visitors coming to the site every month in search of answers. It can be a highly satisfying and rewarding experience to be part of it. P.S. Sure, rude people, online trolls and AI-written answers are annoying. But it makes your personal human touch and humor much more valuable!

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Are Russians surprised that they didn't take Kyiv "in three days"?
Answer: There were countless statements by Russian propagandists that “taking Kyiv will only take 2–3 days”. Even Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko made such a statement. In March 2022, Putin himself ensured Russians that “there will be no need for mobilization” — only to announce mobilization 6 months later. So, yes, Russians indeed were expecting that their troops will just march on Kyiv and have a parade in the afternoon. The coping strategy of Russian propagandists is to claim that: The current slogan on billboards in Russia, “Our victory is inevitable.” I’d like to see how Russian propagandists will explain it when Russia loses Crimea and Donbas. Probably, they will say that NATO tried to liquidate Russia as a state, but Russia managed to remain on the globe, and therefore it won.
